title: Plain ribbed fingerless mitts
subtitle: 1×1 ribbed mitts worked in the round on magic loop.
excerpt: Fingerless mitts in DK wool worked entirely in 1×1 rib, with an afterthought thumb that keeps the stitch count simple on the needles. Sized for hand circumferences of 18, 20, and 22 cm. A good first pair of mitts after a scarf.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 7th series (1880s), §Mittens. The plain ribbed fingerless mitt appears in several Weldon's volumes; the 1×1 rib construction with an afterthought thumb is the most widely reproduced variant. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), §Mitts and gloves, covers the same structure with afterthought thumb instructions.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 30 rounds = 10 × 10 cm in stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Hand circumference 18 (20, 22) cm with 1 to 2 cm negative ease. Hand length from wrist crease to top of cuff 22 (23, 24) cm.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thumb opening made by knitting across the thumb stitches in waste yarn, then returning to them after the hand is complete. The waste yarn is removed to expose live stitches above and below the gap, which are then picked up and worked into the thumb.

A method of knitting small circumferences in the round on a single long circular needle. The cable is pulled out into a large loop at the midpoint of the stitches, splitting the work in half so each half sits on its own needle tip.

content.text: Plain ribbed fingerless mitts in DK wool, worked in the round on magic loop, sized to fit hand circumferences of 18, 20, and 22 cm.
The construction is seamless, worked in the round from cuff to hand top using
magic loop
on a long circular. This avoids any seam running down the palm where wear would show. The thumb uses the
afterthought thumb

method: a short length of waste yarn marks the thumb position while you work the hand, and the thumb is worked separately afterwards. There are no thumb increases to track while the hand is on the needles, which is why this construction is the recommended starting point for first-time mitt knitters. Budget about 100 g (220 m / 240 yards) of DK yarn for both mitts. These fit well under coat cuffs for cold-weather walking.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 100 g (about 220 m / 240 yards) of DK-weight yarn
items.substitutions: Any DK-weight wool or wool blend. A wool content of at least 50% gives the best elasticity in the rib. Pure acrylic is workable but the rib sits less sprightly.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 3.75 mm (UK 9 / US 5) circular needle, at least 80 cm cable, for magic loop
items.substitutions: Double-pointed needles in the same size also work. Use four or five DPNs and divide the stitches evenly across them.

items.name: Stitch markers
items.qty: 2 — one for the beginning of the round, one to mark the thumb position

items.name: Waste yarn
items.qty: About 40 cm of smooth contrasting yarn for the afterthought thumb marker

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 30 rounds to 10 cm over stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked. 1×1 rib at the same needle size pulls in to approximately the same stitch count when worn, so the stocking-stitch swatch gives a reliable working gauge.

If your gauge runs tight by one stitch per 10 cm (23 stitches instead of 22), the finished mitt at size M will be about 1 cm narrower at the palm. For a 20 cm hand that is still wearable, but a 18 cm hand would find the mitt uncomfortably tight. Swatch first and move up a needle size if needed.
Stitches used

items.name: k1, p1
items.qty: 1×1 rib: knit one, purl one, repeated across

content.text: Pattern
Before you cast on, circle your size in the figures below. Every stitch count and measurement reads S (M, L).
Cast on and cuff

Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 36 (40, 44) stitches. For the long-tail method, pull off a tail before starting: the formula is tail_cm = (needle circumference in mm × stitch count) / 10 + 15. At 3.75 mm needles and 44 stitches (the largest size), that is (3.75 × 44) / 10 + 15 = 31.5 cm. Add a little extra for good measure.

Divide the stitches evenly onto the two needle tips for magic loop: 18 (20, 22) on each tip. Join to work in the round, placing the beginning-of-round marker between the last and first stitch. Take care not to twist the cast-on edge before joining.
Work 1×1 rib (k1, p1 every round) for 24 (26, 28) rounds. The cuff measures about 8 (9, 9.5) cm.
Hand to thumb position
Continue in 1×1 rib for a further 8 (10, 12) rounds. The work from the cast-on edge now measures about 11 (12, 13) cm.
Thumb marker

The thumb sits on the right side of the right mitt (and the left side of the left mitt). On a right mitt, the thumb stitches sit at the beginning of the round. Thread a length of waste yarn onto the needle and knit the first 9 (10, 11) stitches of the round with the waste yarn. Slide those stitches back to the left needle and knit them again with the main yarn, continuing in 1×1 rib to the end of the round. The waste yarn marks where the thumb will go; the stitches themselves are still on the main yarn. Place the thumb-position marker on the waste-yarn side to remind you.
Hand above the thumb
Continue in 1×1 rib for a further 12 (14, 16) rounds. The total length from the cast-on edge is now about 19 (21, 23) cm.
Bind off
Bind off all 36 (40, 44) stitches in 1×1 rib: *k1, p1, pass first stitch over second*; repeat to end. Cut the yarn and draw the tail through the last loop.

Stitch count check-in: you should have 36 (40, 44) stitches before binding off. If the count is different, check that no stitches were accidentally dropped or accidentally doubled at the magic-loop join.
Thumb

Remove the waste yarn from the thumb opening by unpicking it stitch by stitch. As you remove each stitch, slip the live loop onto the needle: 9 (10, 11) loops above the gap (these were the original stitches), and 9 (10, 11) loops below the gap (from the strand laid across when the waste yarn was worked in). Total: 18 (20, 22) thumb stitches.
Join the yarn and work 10 (12, 12) rounds of 1×1 rib across all 18 (20, 22) thumb stitches. Bind off in 1×1 rib.

Stitch count check-in: after picking up the thumb stitches, you should have 18 (20, 22) sts in total on the needles. A 2-stitch shortfall usually means a loop was dropped at the top corner of the gap.
Mirror your second mitt

For the second mitt, the thumb opening moves to the opposite side. Work the cuff and hand as above. When you reach the thumb-marker round, work to the last 9 (10, 11) stitches of the round before placing the waste yarn. Hold the first mitt palm-out: the thumb sits on your right. The second mitt's thumb should sit on your left. If both thumbs end up on the same side, you have knitted two right mitts.
Common faults
Two mitts for the same hand: the most common beginner error. Mirror the thumb placement as described above before starting the second mitt.
Cuff too loose after one wash: the cast-on edge was bound off rather than the top, or the cast-on was worked much looser than the body. Work the long-tail cast-on at the same tension as the body rib.

Holes at the thumb corners: the pick-up missed the corner stitch at the gap. When picking up thumb stitches, pick up one extra stitch at each of the two corners and decrease it away on the first thumb round.

Twisted stitch at the join: after pulling the cable loop through, the first stitch can end up twisted. Check it faces the right way before knitting. A twisted stitch sits with its leading leg at the back of the needle instead of the front.
Finishing

Weave all ends in on the wrong side of the mitt: the join at the beginning of the round, the thumb yarn tails, and the cast-on and bind-off tails. Palms and thumb seams take friction, so weave in a good 5 cm in each direction.

Wet-block if using wool: soak in cool water for 10 minutes, squeeze out gently without wringing, and lay flat on a blocking mat. Ease the ribbed sections to the stated measurements. Blocking opens the fabric slightly and sets the stitch definition. Air dry flat before wearing.
Care
Wool: hand wash in cool water with a wool-safe detergent, or machine-wash on a delicate cycle at 30 degrees if the yarn label permits. Lay flat to dry. Do not wring or tumble dry.
Wool-acrylic blends: follow the more restrictive care instructions on the label. Most blends are hand-wash safe at 30 degrees.
What to try next

Once the ribbed fingerless mitt is comfortable, a natural next step is a full mitten with the same afterthought thumb, which adds only the top-decrease shaping. From there, a cabled fingerless mitt introduces the 4-stitch front cable down the back of the hand.
